references.text: The cloud that led the people of Israel through the wilderness is the same cloud that now covers the tabernacle, showing God's enduring presence with his people.
The glory of the Lord (כְבוֹד יְהוָה) settled on Mount Sinai, covered by the cloud, in the same way that the glory now fills the tabernacle.
God's promise to meet the people of Israel at the tabernacle and sanctify it with his glory is fulfilled here.
The Lord's appearance in the cloud above the mercy seat confirms his presence in the tabernacle.
The cloud that covered the tabernacle continued to be a visible sign of God's presence throughout the wilderness journey.
At the dedication of Solomon's temple, the cloud and the glory of the Lord filled the temple just as they did at the tabernacle.
The parallel account in Chronicles describes how the glory of the Lord filled the temple, just as it did at the tabernacle.
Isaiah's vision of the glory of the Lord filling the temple reflects the glory that filled the tabernacle.
Ezekiel's vision shows the cloud and the glory of the Lord in the temple, linking back to the dedication of the tabernacle.
In Ezekiel's vision of the new temple, the glory of the Lord returns and fills the house, just as it did at the tabernacle.
The Word (Logos) who became flesh and took up residence (ἐσκήνωσεν - pitched his tent) among us, and we saw his glory (δόξα), is a fulfillment of God's glory that filled the tabernacle.
The temple in heaven is filled with smoke from God's glory, reflecting the cloud and glory that filled the tabernacle.
God's dwelling (σκηνή) among humanity in the new Jerusalem is the final fulfillment of God's presence that began at the tabernacle.
Repetition of the dedication scene: The cloud covers the tent and the glory of the Lord appears both at its erection and on later occasions.
Theological parallel: The dedication of Solomon's temple repeats the pattern from the dedication of the Tent of Meeting where the cloud fills the sanctuary.
Contrasting parallel: Ezekiel shows the departure of glory as a sign of judgment, in contrast to the fullness of consecration in Exodus.
Consequence of God's presence: The priests' service is halted because the sanctuary is filled with the Lord's glory.
Confirmation of the parallel: Solomon's temple experiences the same overwhelming glory that prevents priestly service.
Complementary account: Describes the same event with an addition about the manifestation of fire in the evening.
Functional contrast: The lifting of the cloud to let the people depart is the direct consequence of its first covering the tent.
Extension of the principle: The duration of the cloud over the tent governs Israel's stay and departure.
